papers.title_in_file: Attendee Guide: A Self-Paced Quantum Learning Journey (Quantum Explorers, July 2023 - February 2024)
papers.what_it_is: IBM's attendee guide to its Quantum Explorers beginner program (July 2023 to February 2024): badges, timeline, credentials, Discord and Jupyter usage, and FAQ; a program logistics document with no technical results.

assertions.value: The guide describes Quantum Explorers as a self-paced, game-based quantum computing learning program for high school students and above, and as a beginner-level program.
assertions.anchor: About the Quantum Explorers Program, p.3
quotes: Quantum Explorers is a self-paced, gamebased quantum computing learning program for high school students and above.
This is a beginner-level program for people interested in quantum computing.
assertions.certainty_reason: IBM describing its own program.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints 'gamebased'; the value reads it as 'game-based'.

assertions.value: The guide gives the program period as July 2023 to February 2024, and says Discord goes to read-only mode in February.
assertions.anchor: Cover page and Timeline, p.1 and p.6
quotes: JULY 2023 - FEBRUARY 2024
DISCORD ON READ-ONLY MODE
assertions.certainty_reason: The guide's own statement of the program's scope in time.
assertions.reader_inference: The timeline graphic is flattened in the text layer, so the pairing of 'read-only mode' with February rests on the layout order and the cover dates.

assertions.value: The guide states that there are seven themed achievements to unlock, with corresponding badges to collect, in two categories: learning badges and community badges.
assertions.anchor: About the Quantum Explorers Program, p.3; About Achievements, p.4
quotes: There are seven themed achievements to unlock, with corresponding badges to collect.
There are two types of space exploration themed badge achievements: learning and community.
assertions.certainty_reason: The guide defines its own achievement structure.

assertions.value: The guide states that Explorers will gain a high-level understanding of quantum computing and some of its applications, and will program real quantum computers.
assertions.anchor: About the Quantum Explorers Program, p.3
quotes: Participants (Explorers) will gain a high-level understanding of quantum computing, some of its applications, and
program real quantum computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: A stated outcome with no evidence of learner results in the guide.
assertions.reader_inference: The two quotes are consecutive lines of one sentence; the text layer breaks the sentence across a column break.

assertions.value: The guide lists seven badges with these topics: Captain (Quantum Computing & Qiskit 101), Time Traveler (Quantum Error Correction & Mitigation), Space Combatant (Quantum Machine Learning), Expert Navigator (Quantum Optimization), Eminent Scientist (Quantum Women Invited Talks), Prime Ambassador (Discord Activity & Community Events) and Supreme Observer (IBM Quantum Challenge Fall 2023).
quotes: Quantum Computing & Qiskit 101 #q-computing-101
Quantum Error Correction & Mitigation #q-error-cm
Quantum Machine Learning #q-machine-learning
Quantum Optimization #q-optimization
Quantum Women Invited Talks #q-women-invited-talks
Discord Activity & Community Events #q-prime-ambassador
IBM Quantum Challenge Fall 2023 #ibmq-challenge
assertions.certainty_reason: The guide's own statement of the program's topics.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer lists badge names and topics as two separate runs; the name-to-topic pairing follows list order, and the one-to-one pairing is the reader's reading of the flattened layout. The KEY (learning versus community) colors are not in the text, so which badge is which type is not stated in the extracted text.

assertions.value: The guide states that total materials cover approximately 50 to 85 hours and that the level of engagement depends on the participant.
quotes: Total materials cover approximately 50 to 85 hours.
Level of engagement depends on you.
assertions.certainty_reason: IBM's estimate of its own program's workload.

assertions.value: The guide states that only the Captain badge is available at program launch, and that dates and times may change during the program, with the #announcements channel the best source of updates.
quotes: Only the Captain badge will be available at program launch.
Dates and times may be subject to change throughout the course of the program.
assertions.certainty_reason: The guide's own stated limit on the timeline.

assertions.value: The guide names these events in its timeline: the Global Quantum Game Jam and the Quantum Explorers Quantum Creative Winter Fest.
quotes: EVENT: GLOBAL QUANTUM GAME JAM
EVENT: QUANTUM EXPLORERS QUANTUM CREATIVE WINTER
assertions.certainty_reason: Event names from a flattened graphic; their dates are not in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The second event name continues on the next line of the text layer ('FEST'); the name is read as 'Quantum Explorers Quantum Creative Winter Fest'.

assertions.value: The guide states that each learning badge has a quiz assessment in its jupyter notebook that must be passed with a score of at least 80 percent, and that a password is revealed on successful completion.
assertions.anchor: How to Unlock a Badge Achievement, Step 3, p.7
quotes: Each learning badge has a quiz assessment in its jupyter notebook that you must pass by achieving a score percentage of at least 80%.
A password will be revealed on successful completion.
assertions.certainty_reason: The guide's own statement of its assessment rule.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says 'score percentage of at least 80%'; the paper does not describe the quiz questions, so the assessment's difficulty is not stated.

assertions.value: The guide states that each community badge has a single question that assesses a string password provided when the participant is eligible, and that passwords must not be shared because they prove an achievement was unlocked.
assertions.anchor: How to Unlock a Badge Achievement, Step 3, p.7
quotes: Each community badge has a single question that assesses a string password that you will be provided when you are eligible to unlock the badge.
Do NOT share the passwords with anyone!
assertions.certainty_reason: The guide's own statement of its verification rule.

assertions.value: The guide states that admins verify an achievement after the participant shares progress in the #level-up channel, and that this can take up to five working days.
assertions.anchor: How to Unlock a Badge Achievement, Step 4, p.8
quotes: Please allow up to five working days for admins to verify your achievement and add the Discord label to your name.
assertions.certainty_reason: The guide's own statement of its verification process.

assertions.value: The guide states the eligibility criteria for IBM digital credentials issued via Credly: Participant needs 1/3 community achievements, Foundational needs 1/4 learning achievements, Intermediate needs 4/4 learning achievements, and Advanced needs 7/7 total achievements.
quotes: Participant - 1/3 community achievements
Foundational - 1/4 learning achievements
Intermediate - 4/4 learning achievements
Advanced - 7/7 total achievements
assertions.certainty_reason: The guide defines its own credential criteria.
assertions.reader_inference: The text writes the criteria as '1/3' and '1/4'; read with 'Advanced - 7/7', these appear to mean at least one of three community badges and at least one of four learning badges, but the guide does not spell out that reading. Counts also imply four learning and three community badges, which the guide's badge list does not mark in the text layer.

assertions.value: The guide states in its FAQ that a participant must achieve the rank of Captain before starting the other learning module badges, and states in the Discord section that unlocking Captain opens the rest of the server and more channels.
assertions.anchor: FAQ, p.18; How to Navigate Discord, Helpful Channels and Roles, p.13
quotes: You’ll need to achieve the rank of Captain before being able to start the other learning module Badges.
Once you unlock the rank of Captain, the rest of the server and more channels will be available to you.
assertions.certainty_reason: The guide's own stated precondition.
assertions.reader_inference: Page 7 says participants may choose any order of badges and that Captain first is encouraged, and the FAQ on p.18 says only Captain is required first. The guide is internally consistent on the exception for Captain.

assertions.value: The guide states that to enter the Discord server a participant must confirm registration for the 2023-24 cohort and being above the age of 14.
assertions.anchor: How to Navigate Discord, Step 2, p.10
quotes: asks if you have registered for the 2023-24 cohort of Quantum Explorers and are above the age of 14.
assertions.certainty_reason: The guide's own stated entry condition.
assertions.reader_inference: The program is described as for 'high school students and above' on p.3; the guide gives no reconciliation of that audience with the age-14 confirmation.

assertions.value: The guide states that the lab exercises are jupyter notebooks that run in the IBM Quantum Lab, a cloud-based jupyter notebook environment, and that notebooks from the Quantum Explorers GitHub repository are downloaded and uploaded to the Lab after logging in to an IBM Quantum Platform account.
assertions.anchor: Using Jupyter Notebooks in the Cloud, p.14 and p.15
quotes: These can be run in the IBM Quantum Lab, which is a cloud-based jupyter notebook environment.
Once you’ve logged into your IBM Quantum Platform account, go to the Lab.
assertions.certainty_reason: IBM describing its own platform.

assertions.value: The guide states that Qiskit is an open source Python framework used to program quantum computers, and that it can be used locally after installing it or in the cloud through the Lab on IBM Quantum Platform.
quotes: Qiskit is an open source Python framework used to program quantum computers.
or you can use it in the cloud without installing it by accessing the Lab on IBM Quantum Platform.
assertions.certainty_reason: IBM describing its own product.

assertions.value: The guide states that all lectures and invited talks will be recorded and available for the duration of the program, that live social events will not be recorded, and that participants may not publicly share most program materials (workbooks, guidebooks, live event recordings, Discord screenshots) but may post their unlocked badge images.
quotes: All lectures and invited talks will be recorded and available for viewing at any time for the duration of the Quantum Explorers program.
Live social events will not be recorded
You cannot upload and publicly share our learning materials like the workbooks, guidebooks, live event recordings, screenshots of our Discord server, etc.
assertions.certainty_reason: The guide's own stated terms of use.
assertions.reader_inference: The guide's material is restricted to registered attendees, so the technical content of the program (including the Quantum Machine Learning module) is not in this document and cannot be checked from it.

assertions.value: The guide states that top performing Explorers will be highlighted at the end of the program.
assertions.anchor: About the Quantum Explorers Program, p.3
quotes: Top performing Explorers will be highlighted at the end of the program.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of intent; the guide gives no ranking criterion.

papers.title_in_file: Redefining Randomness: Quantis QRNG PCIe-40M & PCIe-240M (Product Brochure)
papers.what_it_is: A two-page ID Quantique product brochure, dated April 2021, for the Quantis PCIe-40M and PCIe-240M quantum random number generator cards.

assertions.value: The vendor states that the Quantis PCIe-40M and PCIe-240M embed IDQ20MC1 chips, which generate randomness from the shot noise of a light source captured by a CMOS image sensor.
quotes: Quantis PCIe-40M and PCIe-240M embed IDQ20MC1 chips
generate randomness from the shot noise of a light source captured by a CMOS image sensor
assertions.reader_inference: A brochure description of the product's entropy source; no design detail, entropy model or measurement is given.

assertions.value: The vendor states that the cards can generate random bits directly from the entropy source (entropy data mode), or after NIST compliant post-processing (RNG data mode).
quotes: They can generate random bits directly from the entropy source (entropy data mode), or after a NIST compliant post-processing (RNG data mode).

assertions.value: The vendor's table lists the PCIe-40M with a quantum entropy source rate of 38.3 Mbps plus or minus 5% and an RNG data output (embedded NIST compliant DRBG) of 9.6 Mbps plus or minus 5%.
assertions.anchor: Page 2 (table 'Quantis QRNG modules at a glance'), PERFORMANCE
quotes: PERFORMANCE Quantum entropy source
RNG Data Output (embedded NIST compliant DRBG)
9.6 Mbps ± 5%
assertions.reader_inference: Column assignment (first value to PCIe-40M, second to PCIe-240M) follows the order of the text layer; the table header lists PCIe-40M first. The RNG output is about a quarter of the raw entropy rate on both models. The brochure gives no measurement conditions.

assertions.value: The vendor's table lists the PCIe-240M with a quantum entropy source rate of 232 Mbps plus or minus 5% and an RNG data output (embedded NIST compliant DRBG) of 58 Mbps plus or minus 5%.
assertions.anchor: Page 2 (table 'Quantis QRNG modules at a glance'), PERFORMANCE
quotes: PERFORMANCE Quantum entropy source
232 Mbps ± 5%
RNG Data Output (embedded NIST compliant DRBG)
58 Mbps ± 5%
assertions.reader_inference: Column assignment follows the order of the text layer; PCIe-240M is the second column. The brochure gives no measurement conditions.

assertions.value: The vendor states that the new PCIe-40M and PCIe-240M are compliant with NIST SP800 90A/B/C recommendations and pass IID, non-IID tests, DieHarder and NIST SP800-22 test suites.
quotes: are compliant with NIST SP800 90A/B/C recommendations and passes IID, non-IID tests, DieHarder and NIST SP800-22 test suites
assertions.reader_inference: The brochure reports no test output, p-values, entropy estimates or lab name, so the compliance statement cannot be checked from this document.

assertions.value: The vendor's table marks NIST SP800-90A/B/C, SP800-22 and DieHarder test suite compliance as supported for both models.
assertions.anchor: Page 2 (table 'Quantis QRNG modules at a glance'), CERTIFICATIONS
quotes: NIST SP800-90A/B/C, SP800-22 and DieHarder test suite compliance
assertions.reader_inference: The check marks are glyphs that the text layer prints as a single character per cell; both model columns carry one.

assertions.value: The vendor states that METAS and CC certifications of the two new products are under way, and the table lists BSI Common Criteria and AIS 31 certification as pending for both models.
assertions.anchor: Page 1, Compliant and certified; Page 2 (table 'Quantis QRNG modules at a glance'), CERTIFICATIONS
quotes: METAS and CC certifications of these two new products are under way.
BSI Common Criteria & AIS 31 certification
assertions.reader_inference: As of the April 2021 specification date, neither card holds a third-party certification according to this document.

assertions.value: The vendor states that legacy Quantis PCIe and USB products have been certified by leading commercial entities, well-known international institutes and governments worldwide, and that they also present an AIS31 version compliant with the German BSI's AIS31 validation criteria.
quotes: Legacy Quantis PCIe and USB have been certified by leading commercial entities, well-known international institutes and governments worldwide.
Legacy PCIe and USB also present an AIS31 version that is compliant with the German BSI
assertions.reader_inference: No certificate numbers or issuing bodies are named.

assertions.value: The vendor states that live status verification and entropy source health monitoring performed at chip level ensure the cards always provide the highest entropy, and that any failure or attacks are detected.
quotes: Live status verification and entropy source health monitoring performed at chip level ensure the PCie cards always provide the highest entropy, and any failure or attacks are detected.
assertions.reader_inference: The brochure names no health tests, thresholds or attack model; 'any ... attacks are detected' is an unquantified claim.

assertions.value: The vendor states that only Quantum Random Number Generators (QRNGs) are intrinsically random and provably unpredictable.
quotes: Only Quantum Random Number Generators (QRNGs) are intrinsically random and provably unpredictable
assertions.reader_inference: A marketing statement with no proof or reference in the brochure. It is stronger than the usual physics position, where the guarantee of a real device depends on how well the device is modelled and on its noise and classical contributions.

assertions.value: The vendor describes the Quantis family as exploiting elementary quantum optic processes that are fundamentally probabilistic to produce true randomness, and lists a provably secure source of entropy as a reason to choose Quantis QRNGs.
assertions.anchor: Page 1, Provably secure; page 2, Why choose Quantis QRNGs?
quotes: The Quantis QRNG family exploits elementary quantum optic processes that are fundamentally probabilistic to produce true randomness.
Provably secure source of entropy
assertions.reader_inference: The brochure gives no security proof or security definition; 'provably secure' is not backed in this document.

assertions.value: The vendor states that the quantum processes underlying the QRNG are well understood and characterized, so their inner working can be modelled and controlled to produce the highest entropy from the first bit.
quotes: As the quantum processes underlying the QRNG are well understood and characterized, their inner working can be clearly modelized and controlled to produce the highest entropy from the first bit.

assertions.value: The vendor's table gives the thermal noise contribution as below 1%, defined as the fraction of random bits arising from thermal noise.
assertions.anchor: Page 2 (table 'Quantis QRNG modules at a glance'), ENVIRONMENTAL
quotes: Thermal noise contribution
<1% (fraction of random bits arising from thermal noise)
assertions.reader_inference: This implies that a small share of output bits is classical in origin, which the headline statement of intrinsic randomness does not mention. The brochure does not say how the figure was measured.

assertions.value: The vendor's table gives a storage temperature range of -40 °C to +85 °C and an operating temperature range of 0 °C to +50 °C for both models.
assertions.anchor: Page 2 (table 'Quantis QRNG modules at a glance'), ENVIRONMENTAL
quotes: Storage temperature
Operating temperature
0 °C to +50 °C

assertions.value: The vendor's table gives the card dimensions as 80 x 63.75 mm for both models, and the specification as PCI Express Base 1.0a compliant.
assertions.anchor: Page 2 (table 'Quantis QRNG modules at a glance'), PHYSICAL CHARACTERISTICS
quotes: PHYSICAL CHARACTERISTICS Dimensions (mm)
PCI Express Base 1.0a compliant

assertions.value: The vendor's table lists support of the Quantis library and EasyQuantis application on Windows 10 and Ubuntu 18.04 for both models.
assertions.anchor: Page 2 (table 'Quantis QRNG modules at a glance'), OS SUPPORTED
quotes: OS SUPPORTED (QUANTIS LIBRARY AND EASYQUANTIS APPLICATION)*
Windows 10
Ubuntu 18.04

assertions.value: The vendor states that the Quantis library produces random binary data, integers and floating point numbers, can access multiple Quantis generators, and includes random data scaling; that the Quantis extensions libraries implement a randomness extractor for post-processing the output; and that the Easy Quantis application reads and displays random numbers or stores them in a file.
assertions.anchor: Page 2 (table 'Quantis QRNG modules at a glance'), footnote (*)
quotes: Quantis library enables the production of random binary data, integers and floating point numbers.
The Quantis extensions libraries implement a randomness extractor which can be used to postprocess the output of the Quantis QRNG.
Easy Quantis application allow to read and display random numbers or store them in a file.

assertions.value: The vendor states that the Quantis QRNG family has been commonly used since 2001 as a trusted source of randomness, for key generation for cryptographic modules, access protection for networks, servers, virtual machines and applications, data integrity and confidentiality, gaming, and scientific simulations or modeling.
quotes: Since 2001, the Quantis QRNG family is commonly used as trusted source of randomness for multiple applications
assertions.reader_inference: No customer, deployment count or audit is given.

assertions.value: The vendor's applications list names Artificial Intelligence (Machine and Deep Learning) as one application area, alongside confidentiality and integrity of sensitive data, security of end-consumer devices, scientific modeling and simulations, financial transactions and blockchain, and gaming and random drawings.
quotes: Artificial Intelligence (Machine and Deep Learning)
Financial transactions / Blockchain
Scientific Modeling & Simulations
assertions.reader_inference: Only a list entry; the brochure gives no description of how the random bits would be used in ML or any result.

assertions.value: The vendor states that its information and specifications are subject to change at any time without prior notice, and dates the specifications as of April 2021.
quotes: The information and specification set forth in this document are subject to change at any time by ID Quantique without prior notice.
Specifications as of April 2021.
assertions.certainty_reason: The document's own disclaimer states the date and the scope of its specifications.
assertions.reader_inference: Every figure above is a vendor figure as of April 2021 and may have changed.

papers.title_in_file: Efficient Light Generation in Ultraviolet-A Band on Chip
papers.version_note: arXiv:2504.07009v1, compiled April 10, 2025; text layer has flat exponents and garbled equations (1) to (4).
papers.what_it_is: A letter reporting second harmonic generation of 770.08 nm light into 385.04 nm in a periodically poled thin-film lithium niobate waveguide with a measured normalized efficiency of 1797 %W-1cm-2.

assertions.value: The authors report an internal second harmonic generation efficiency of 1797 %W−1/cm−2 for light generated in the Ultraviolet-A band in a periodically poled lithium niobate waveguide, which they describe as a 9.1-times improvement over the state of the art.
quotes: Here we demonstrate light generation in the Ultraviolet-A band in a periodic poled waveguide via second harmonic generation.
The internal efficiency reaches 1797 %W−1/cm−2, marking a 9.1-times improvement over the state of art, thanks to better mode overlap and poling.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-device empirical result with a loss calibration the authors say it depends on.
assertions.reader_inference: The 9.1 factor is relative to the 197 %W-1cm-2 result at 355 nm (Ref. 5) only; see the comparison-table assertion.

assertions.value: The authors state that they use a periodically poled lithium niobate on insulator waveguide that is quasi-phase matched for second harmonic generation of 770.08 nm into 385.04 nm.
quotes: We use a periodic poled LNOI waveguide that is quasi-phase matched for the second harmonic generation (SHG) of 770.08 nm into 385.04 nm.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own device and operating wavelengths in the introduction.
assertions.reader_inference: The design section and Table 1 give 780 nm into 390 nm instead of 770.08 nm into 385.04 nm; the paper does not reconcile the two sets of wavelengths.

assertions.value: The authors define the Ultraviolet-A band as the part of the spectrum spanning between 320 nm and 400 nm, at the left edge of the visible spectrum.
quotes: Ultraviolet-A (UV-A) band lies to the left edge of the visible spectrum, spanning between 320 nm and 400 nm.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition given in the paper's introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that silica waveguides have been used to generate light from 322 nm to 545 nm and lithium tantalate microdisks have been used to generate 384 nm light, and that both suffer low efficiency.
quotes: silica waveguides have been used to generate light ranging from 322 nm to 545 nm [13], and lithium tantalate microdisks have been used to generate 384 nm light [14], but they suffer low efficiency.
assertions.certainty_reason: Attributed to Refs. 13 and 14; no numbers for their efficiencies are given.

assertions.value: The authors state that short-wavelength light generation in lithium niobate on insulator has only countable demonstrations, at 435 nm, 456 nm and, most recently in the UV-A band, at 355 nm, and that the 355 nm demonstration had a low efficiency of 197 %W−1cm−2.
quotes: with only countable demonstrations at 435 nm [12], 456 nm [11], and most recently in the UV-A band at 355 nm [5], although the latter had a low efficiency at 197%W−1cm−2.
assertions.certainty_reason: Attributed to Refs. 5, 11 and 12.

assertions.value: The authors state that their technique can find applications in atomic clocks, frequency comb generation, sensing, and visible entanglement generation.
quotes: Our technique can find applications in atomic clocks, frequency comb generation, sensing, and visible entanglement generation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Prospective application statement; no application is demonstrated in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results and further developments would open doors to powerful applications in atomic clocks, quantum memory and quantum sensing, where photonic integrated circuits could provide much practical value.
quotes: Our results and further developments would open doors to powerful applications in atomic clocks, quantum memory, quantum sensing, and so on, where photonic integrated circuits could provide much practical values.
assertions.certainty_reason: Prospective statement without evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper builds no quantum-computing device or protocol; its bearing on quantum computing is as a component technology (UV light source) only.

assertions.value: The authors report that, for a top width of 1.4 µm, a sidewall angle of 64 degrees and an etching depth of 350 nm, the poling period is calculated to be 1.71 µm for second harmonic generation of 780 nm into 390 nm.
quotes: For a top width of 1.4 µm, a side-wall angle of 64◦, and an etching depth of 350 nm, the poling period is calculated to be 1.71 µm for SHG of 780 nm to 390 nm.
assertions.certainty_reason: Design calculation from finite-difference eigenmode simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: This design wavelength pair (780 nm to 390 nm) differs from the measured 770.08 nm to 385.04 nm.

assertions.value: The authors define the effective nonlinear coefficient as 2 d33 divided by pi, with d33 the nonlinear susceptibility of lithium niobate, and compute the normalized conversion efficiency from simulated transverse electric modes, the waveguide length of 3.5 mm, and a mode overlap factor.
quotes: Using these modes, we can compute the conversion efficiency
L is the length of the waveguide (3.5 mm
de f f is 2d33/π, with d33 being the susceptibility of lithium niobate χ(2).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the quantities of its efficiency model (Eq. 1) in Section 2.
assertions.reader_inference: The equations are garbled in the text layer; only the prose definitions are quoted.

assertions.value: The authors report simulated mode cross-sectional areas of 0.55 µm squared for the second harmonic and 0.66 µm squared for the pump, giving a mode overlap factor of 0.97, which they call nearly perfect.
quotes: our calculation finds A2ω = 0.55µm2, Aω = 0.66µm2, to give nearly-perfect mode overlap ξ = 0.97
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result; exponent printed flat in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors report a theoretical second harmonic generation efficiency of 10467 %W−1cm−2 for ideal poling with a 50:50 duty cycle.
quotes: the theoretical SHG efficiency η is 10467 %W−1cm−2. This result is for an ideal poling with a 50:50
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result for an ideal poling condition.

assertions.value: The authors report that the fabricated poling shows a 35:65 duty cycle, which they state reduces the simulated efficiency 3.6-times to 2905 %W−1cm−2.
quotes: showing a 35:65 duty cycle. This leads to a 3.6-times decrease in the simulated efficiency, to 2905 %W−1cm−2.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result for the measured duty cycle.

assertions.value: The authors report that the waveguide is fabricated on an X-cut thin film lithium niobate wafer with a 600 nm thick lithium niobate film bonded to a 2 µm thermally grown silicon dioxide layer above a silicon substrate.
quotes: The waveguide is fabricated on an X-Cut thin film lithium niobate (TFLN) wafer (NANOLN Inc.), which is a 600 nm thick lithium niobate (LN) thin film bonded to a 2 µm thermally grown silicon dioxide layer above a silicon substrate.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own device platform.

assertions.value: The authors describe the process: gold and chromium electrodes of 60 nm and 30 nm are deposited, the waveguide areas are periodically poled with high-voltage pulses, the waveguide is patterned by electron beam lithography with 850 nm hydrogen silsesquioxane resist, etched with inductively coupled plasma to 350 nm leaving a 250 nm slab, and capped with a thin silicon dioxide layer by plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition.
quotes: The gold and chromium layers are then deposited with an electron-beam evaporator (AJA, Orion-8E), with a thickness of 60 nm and 30 nm, respectively.
The waveguide areas are then periodically poled by applying high-voltage pulses onto the electrode pads.
after the 850 nm hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) resist is spun on the thin film
The etching depth is set to 350 nm, resulting in a 250 nm remaining slab layer.
Lastly, a thin layer of silicon dioxide is applied using plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper describes its own fabrication process.
assertions.reader_inference: The 100 keV electron beam energy for the waveguide pattern is in the same paragraph but is not quoted here.

assertions.value: The authors report a fabricated periodically poled waveguide with 1.4 µm top width, 350 nm etching depth, 64 degree sidewall angle and 1.71 µm design poling period; scanning electron microscope images show poled sectors 0.655 µm and 1.08 µm wide, a 35:65 poling duty cycle, and a measured poling period of 1.706 µm.
quotes: The result is a periodic poled lithium niobate (PPLN) nanowaveguide with 1.4 µm top width, 350 nm etching depth, and 64◦ side-wall angle, and 1.71 µm poling period
each lighter sector 0.655 µm wide, each darker sector 1.08 µm wide
the poling duty cycle (ratio of poled to unpoled) is 35:65.
The measured poling period is 1.706 µm, which is very close to the designed period of 1.71 µm.
assertions.reader_inference: The sector widths 0.655 µm and 1.08 µm sum to 1.735 µm, not to the 1.706 µm measured period; the paper does not comment on the difference.

assertions.value: The authors describe a setup with a tunable laser covering 765 nm to 781 nm, a fiber polarization controller, lensed-fiber coupling of 7.67 dB loss on the input, a chip stage held at 35 degrees Celsius, a collimating aspheric lens, two band-pass filters that reject the pump, and a power meter that measures the generated UV-A light.
quotes: It begins with a wavelength-tunable laser (New Focus, 765-781 nm)
with a measured 7.67 dB loss. The chip is housed on a temperature controlled stage stabilized at 35◦C.
two band-pass filters (Thorlabs, FBH400-40) are inserted to reject the pump, after which the generated UV-A is measured using a power meter (Thorlabs, S130VC).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that a coarse scan of the laser over the laser's full range found a peak generated UV-A power of about 770 nW at around 770.08 nm.
quotes: The peak generated power is about 770 nW, found at around 770.08 nm.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single measurement; the pump power for this scan is not stated in the same sentence.

assertions.value: The authors report a measured phase matching bandwidth of 0.3 nm full width at half maximum, against a simulated 0.1 nm, from a fine scan from 769 nm to 771 nm at 12 mW output power of the laser.
quotes: Then, the measurement is repeated with the laser fine scanning from 769 to 771 nm, while its output power is kept at 12 mW.
the measured phase matching bandwidth has a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 0.3 nm.
In contrast, the simulated FWHM is only 0.1 nm
assertions.reader_inference: The authors attribute the difference to group velocity dispersion changed by fabrication imperfections; a nonuniform poling pattern would also broaden the curve, but the paper does not test either explanation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the difference between the simulated and measured bandwidths indicates a different group velocity dispersion in the experiment than in the simulation, due to fabrication imperfections.
quotes: which indicates the different group velocity dispersion from simulation than experiment, due to fabrication imperfections.
assertions.certainty_reason: Explanation stated without a test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report a laser diode measurement of a total fiber-to-fiber insertion loss of 21.65 dB, assume equal on-chip and off-chip losses of 10.83 dB per facet because the coupling setup is symmetric, and measure the free-space components to add 0.3 dB loss.

the on-chip and off-chip losses are assumed to be the same, which is 10.83 dB per facet.
the total loss of free space components is measured to be 0.3 dB
assertions.reader_inference: The 10.83 dB per facet is an assumption, not a measurement of each facet, and the calibration light is at 400 nm rather than the generated 385.04 nm.

assertions.value: The authors report that the output pump power is mostly linear in the input power with a slight deviation, indicating weak second harmonic generation; a fit gives beta of (2.63 ± 0.18) × 10 to the power of −2 and alpha of (7.7 ± 6.9) × 10 to the power of −3 per mW at 95% confidence, with beta converted to a 15.8 dB loss against a separately measured 15.3 dB, and the fit uncertainty for alpha too high to extract the efficiency.
quotes: the dependence is mostly linear with only a slight deviation, which indicates weak SHG.
finds β = (2.63 ± 0.18) × 10−2 and α = (7.7 ± 6.9) × 10−3/mW, where the uncertainties correspond to a confidence level of 95%.
which is converted to a 15.8
dB loss, consistent with our separately measured loss of 15.3 dB.
Due to the weak SHG, however, the uncertainty from the curve fitting is too high.
assertions.reader_inference: The uncertainty on alpha is about 90% of its value, so the pump-depletion fit alone does not bound the efficiency.

assertions.value: The authors report that, to extract the efficiency, they fit the on-chip second harmonic power as a quadratic function of the on-chip pump power, with the on-chip second harmonic power from the measured power multiplied by a factor printed as 101.098 to correct for off-chip and free-space loss, and the on-chip pump power taken as beta times the input power; the input pump power was swept from 2 mW to 12 mW.
quotes: To reliably extract the conversion efficiency, we instead use the β value from Fig. 5 to fit the generated SH power as

is the on-chip pump power calculated as βPin, to account for the on-chip loss.
as the input pump power is swept from 2 mW to 12 mW.

assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the factor as 101.098; this is likely ten to the power 1.098, which is 10.98 dB, a little below the 10.83 dB plus 0.3 dB (11.13 dB) the loss calibration implies. The paper does not explain the difference.

assertions.value: The authors report a fitted quadratic coefficient gamma of (2.1 ± 0.1) × 10 to the power of −3 per mW, a clear quadratic dependence of second harmonic power on pump power, and a normalized efficiency gamma divided by L squared of 1797 %W−1cm−2.
quotes: a clear quadratic behavior is seen, as opposed to previously reported [5].
The fitting gives γ = (2.1 ± 0.1) × 10−3/mW, with which the normalized efficiency is computed as γ/L2 to give η = 1797%W−1cm−2.
assertions.reader_inference: With L = 3.5 mm, gamma = 2.1e-3 per mW gives about 1714 %W-1cm-2; 1797 corresponds to gamma of about 2.2e-3, inside the stated uncertainty of 0.1e-3.

assertions.value: The authors state that the efficiency value hinges on the accuracy of the 400 nm light loss measurement, which they repeated to verify their results.
quotes: Note that this efficiency value hinges on
the accuracy of the 400-nm light loss measurement, which we repeatedly performed to verify our results.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the dependence of its headline result on one calibration.

assertions.value: The authors report that the simulated efficiency for the 35:65 duty cycle, 2905 %W−1cm−2, is 1.6 times higher than the experimental result, and state that the discrepancy is partially because the simulation does not include waveguide propagation loss and also signifies fabrication imperfections including non-uniform poling and a sidewall angle that deviates from the design.

This discrepancy is partially because our simulation has not taken into account the waveguide propagation loss.
including non-uniform poling patterns and that the side wall angle deviates from the design.
assertions.reader_inference: The propagation loss of the waveguide is not measured in the paper, so its share of the 1.6 factor is not quantified.

assertions.value: The authors list in Table 1 (columns for earlier references and this work) second harmonic generation efficiencies of 33000 %W−1cm−2 at 456.5 nm, about 1040 %W−1cm−2 at 435.5 nm, about 197 %W−1cm−2 at 355 nm, and 1797 %W−1cm−2 at 390 nm for this work.

The table shows 33000 %W-1cm-2 at 456.5 nm, higher than this work, so the record claim holds only for the UV-A band; the table lists 390 nm for this work while the measured pump was 770.08 nm (385.04 nm).

assertions.value: The authors state that they present efficient UV-A light generation on chip with a record high conversion efficiency of 1797 %W−1cm−2, corresponding to a 9.1 times improvement over the state of the art as listed in Table 1.

papers.what_it_is: A 59-page Interviewbit introductory cheat sheet on Python syntax, built-in types, control flow, data structures, standard modules and IPython magic commands.
papers.why_not: The document is a general-purpose Python language tutorial. It states no claim about quantum machine learning, quantum computing, classical machine learning, finance or fraud, or statistical evaluation method. It reports no measurement, theorem or experiment. Its only link to machine learning is the name of a link in the closing list (Machine Learning Interview Questions), which has no content in the document.

papers.title_in_file: PHOTON-PAIR GENERATION IN A HETEROGENEOUS SILICON PHOTONIC CHIP
papers.version_note: arXiv:2208.13955v1, 30 Aug 2022. The text layer holds the paper once, 8 pages. Table 1 is flattened column by column, so its rows are read by column order.
papers.what_it_is: An experimental paper reporting photon-pair and heralded single-photon generation by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a hydrogenated amorphous silicon waveguide routed through low-loss silicon nitride waveguides on one chip.

assertions.value: The authors report a highest coincidence-to-accidental ratio (CAR) of 1632.6 (± 260.4) at an average on-chip pump power of about -30.5 dBm, with a corresponding photon pair generation rate of 1.94 MHz.
quotes: The highest CAR is achieved at 1632.6 (± 260.4) with average on-chip pump power of about -30.5 dBm.
The corresponding photon pair generation rate (PGR) is measured and estimated to be 1.94 MHz.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical result from one device and one run series.
assertions.reader_inference: The CAR is for dark-count-subtracted counts (see the dark-count assertion); the pair rate is derived from singles and coincidence rates (see the PGR definition), not counted directly.

assertions.value: The authors state that the CAR of 1632.6 (± 260.4) is a record high for non-resonant a-Si:H waveguides and a 4-times improvement over the previous single-layer a-Si:H platform.
quotes: we have experimentally demonstrated photon-pair generation with a record high CAR of 1632.6 (± 260.4) for non-resonant a-Si:H waveguides
which shows 4-times improvement compared to the previous single-layer a-Si:H platform
assertions.certainty_reason: A priority and comparison claim by the authors, against one earlier result (Wang et al. 2014) and a table of selected works.
assertions.reader_inference: The record is limited to non-resonant a-Si:H waveguides. Table 1 of the same paper lists higher CAR values for other platforms (see the Table 1 assertion). Table 1 gives 399 for the earlier a-Si:H result, a ratio of 4.09.

assertions.value: The authors state that, against the previous result in a pure a-Si:H platform, their device has 4 times higher CAR and 30 times higher PGR, and they attribute this to much lower propagation and coupling loss through the waveguide.
quotes: our device has exhibited 4 times higher CAR and 30 times higher PGR due to much lower
propagation/coupling loss through the waveguide.
assertions.certainty_reason: The attribution to lower loss is the authors' explanation; the paper does not test it by a control experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 1 gives 65 kHz for the earlier a-Si:H result and 1.94 MHz for this work, a ratio of about 30. The comparison mixes different pump powers, filters and detectors.

assertions.value: The authors report that the CAR drops to 1335.3 (± 240.9) when the on-chip pump power is lowered further, and they explain this by background noise contributing more when the Stokes and anti-Stokes count rates approach the dark-count level.
quotes: The CAR then drops to 1335.3 (± 240.9) when further lowering on-chip pump power.
the background noise contributes more to the result when the count rates of Stokes and anti-Stokes photons are closer to the dark-count level.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical observation with the authors' explanation; the explanation is not tested separately.
assertions.reader_inference: This is a stated limit of the CAR figure: the CAR peaks at an intermediate pump power and is not a monotone function of power.

assertions.value: The authors state that the dark count has been subtracted from the coincidence and accidental counts before the CAR is computed.
quotes: The dark count has been subtracted from coincidence and accidental counts to eliminate dark-count noise
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own data-processing step in Section 2, p.4.
assertions.reader_inference: The quoted CAR values are therefore not raw CAR values and are not directly comparable with works that do not subtract dark counts. The paper does not state whether the compared works in Table 1 did.

assertions.value: The authors define the photon pair generation rate as estimated by N1 times N2 divided by N12, where N1, N2 and N12 are the detection rates of signal, idler and two-photon coincidences.
quotes: The PGR is then estimated as N1N2/N12, where N1, N2 and N12 donates the detection rate of signal, idler and two-photon coincidences.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the estimator in Section 2, p.4.
assertions.reader_inference: The ratio N1N2/N12 uses detected rates only. It is a rate at the source if the signal and idler channels have equal transmission and detection efficiency, which the paper does not state.

assertions.value: The authors report that with an on-chip pump power of -20.5 dBm and a programmable waveshaper in place of the DWDM filters, the CAR remains about 200 for wavelength detuning from 4.2 nm to 10.2 nm, and that the waveshaper adds 5 dB loss which raises the required pump power.
quotes: With on-chip pump power at -20.5 dBm, the CAR remains about 200 for the wavelength detuning from 4.2 nm to 10.2 nm.
The waveshaper introduces an additional 5 dB loss, which increases the required pump power.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical measurement series on one device.
assertions.reader_inference: The 4.2 nm to 10.2 nm span is 6 nm wide.

assertions.value: The authors describe the multi-channel bandwidth differently in three places: the Introduction says a detuning bandwidth of 6 nm, the body text says detuning from 4.2 nm to 10.2 nm, and the Conclusion says a CAR of around 200 across a 10-nm bandwidth.
assertions.anchor: Introduction p.2; Section 2 p.4; Conclusion p.5
quotes: multiple channels with a detuning bandwidth of 6 nm and CAR value consistently at 200
the CAR remains about 200 for the wavelength detuning from 4.2 nm to 10.2 nm
multi-channel photon-pair sources with a CAR of around 200 across 10-nm bandwidth
assertions.certainty_reason: A reading of three statements in one paper; the measured range is in Figure 4(d), which the text layer does not carry.
assertions.reader_inference: The measured span (detuning 4.2 nm to 10.2 nm) is 6 nm wide and its upper end is 10.2 nm, so the Introduction and Conclusion use different readings of one result. The Section 2 statement is the most specific.

assertions.value: The authors report a lowest heralded auto-correlation gH(2)(0) of 0.0126 ± 0.005 at an on-chip power of -22.5 dBm and a signal rate N1 of 18 kHz, rising to 0.1085 ± 0.0014 at -16.3 dBm and N1 of 310 kHz.
quotes: The lowest gH(2)(0) is measured to be 0.0126 ± 0.005 at an on-chip power of -22.5 dBm and N1 of 18 kHz.
It increases to 0.1085 ± 0.0014 at on-chip power of -16.3 dBm and N1 of 310 kHz.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one device.
assertions.reader_inference: The auto-correlation rises with pump power, as expected when multi-pair emission grows. The uncertainty on the lowest value (0.005) is large relative to the value.

assertions.value: The abstract reports a lowest gH(2)(0) of 0.1085 ± 0.0014, whereas the main text gives 0.0126 ± 0.005 as the lowest value, 0.1085 ± 0.0014 as the value at higher power, and the Conclusion gives 0.0125 ± 0.005.
assertions.anchor: Abstract p.1; Section 2 p.4; Conclusion p.5
quotes: Lastly, we measure heralded single-photons with a lowest gH(2)(0) of 0.1085 ± 0.0014.
The lowest gH(2)(0) is measured to be 0.0126 ± 0.005
demonstrated low correlation function of gH(2)(0) at 0.0125 ± 0.005
assertions.certainty_reason: Three statements in one paper disagree; a reader cannot settle which figure is intended from the text alone.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract figure of 0.1085 contradicts the body, where it is the value at higher power. The conclusion's 0.0125 differs from the body's 0.0126 in the last digit. The body and Table 1 (0.0126) agree, so 0.0126 is the best-supported lowest value.

assertions.value: The authors state that gH(2)(τ) is calculated as N123 times N1 divided by N12 times N13, from double coincidences of the signal with idler I (N12) and idler II (N13) and triple coincidences N123, with the idler split by a 50/50 splitter and zero-delay values normalized to the average at other 20 ns delays.
quotes: the idler is separated by a 50/50 splitter into two as idler I and idler II
The auto-correlation function of gH(2)(τ ) is then calculated by N123N1/N12N13, where N1 donates signal detection rate.
which is normalized to the averaged gH(2)(τ ) at other 20 ns-delays (corresponding to the 50 MHz repetition rate of our MLL)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the estimator and normalization in Section 2, p.4.
assertions.reader_inference: The normalization to other pulse delays treats accidental coincidences between pulses as the baseline, so the quoted value is a ratio to that baseline.

assertions.value: The authors state that duplicating the detected photon channel into multiple virtual channels with different time delays lets all corresponding coincidences be measured at once, within the same experimental run, which they say largely simplifies the experiment and reduces noise and instabilities from different runs.
quotes: This is enabled by duplicating the detected physical photon channel to multiple virtual channels with different time delays
This method largely simpli
reduces noise and instabilities induced by different experimental runs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The benefit is an author statement without a comparison measurement.

assertions.value: The authors describe the fabrication: a 100-mm silicon wafer with 3-µm thermal oxide, 240 nm of SiNx by low-pressure chemical vapor deposition at 775 oC, then 225-nm of a-Si:H by plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition at 300 oC, with the a-Si:H waveguides patterned by e-beam lithography and reactive ion etching.
quotes: The device fabrication starts with a 100-mm silicon wafer with a 3-µm thick layer of thermal oxide on its surface. 240 nm of SiNx is deposited using low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LPCVD).
a temperature of 775 oC
225-nm of a-Si:H was then deposited by PECVD.
a temperature of 300 oC
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own fabrication recipe in Section 2, p.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that the lower a-Si:H deposition temperature lets them deposit it directly on top of the SiNx waveguides without damaging them.
quotes: With the lower a-Si:H deposition temperature we are able to deposit it directly on top of the SiNx waveguides without damaging them.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement of the reason for the process choice, without a damage test in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The introduction also cites lower deposition temperature as the reason a-Si:H fits mass chip manufacturing (see the cited Hemsley 2016 statement).

assertions.value: The authors report an on-chip interlayer coupling insertion loss below 1 dB per transition over a 100 nm bandwidth, propagation losses of 0.5 dB/cm in SiNx and 4 dB/cm in a-Si:H, and a total on-off chip loss of 9 dB.
quotes: The on-chip interlayer coupling insertion loss is measured to be less than 1 dB per transition over a 100 nm bandwidth
the propagation losses in the SiNx and a-Si:H waveguides are 0.5 dB/cm and 4 dB/cm, respectively
The total on-off chip loss is 9 dB.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured device figures from one fabrication run.
assertions.reader_inference: The introduction says the coupling loss is optimized around 0.5 dB per transition in the earlier design, while the measured bound here is less than 1 dB per transition.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing their previous work, that a careful design of the vertical coupler optimizes the coupling loss to around 0.5 dB per transition, and that using Si3N4 for on/off-chip coupling dramatically reduces fiber-to-fiber loss and the required pump power.
quotes: With a careful design of vertical coupler, the coupling loss is optimized around 0.5 dB per transition.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to MacFarlane et al. [2019], not measured in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors report a Kerr coefficient of about 5 x 10 to the power of minus 13 square centimeters per watt, equated from degenerate four-wave mixing conversion efficiency measured on devices with a-Si:H lengths between 1 mm and 5.5 mm, and call it comparable to the state-of-the-art value of 7.43 x 10 to the power of minus 13.
quotes: These results equate to a Kerr coefficient of ∼ 5 x 10−13 cm2/W, which is comparable to the state-of-the-art value (7.43 x 10−13 cm2/W)
propagates for varying a-Si:H lengths between 1 mm and 5.5 mm
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical estimate from conversion-efficiency fits; the fit is in Figure 2(b), which the text layer does not carry.
assertions.reader_inference: The measured value is about two thirds of the cited value; whether that is within error is not stated.

assertions.value: The authors cite Wang and Foster for a Kerr nonlinearity of n2 = 7.43 ± 0.87 x 10 to the power of minus 13 square centimeters per watt for a-Si:H, which they call ultra-high compared with other silicon-based platforms, and state that efficient SFWM can then be reached with only millimeters of waveguide propagation.
quotes: its ultra-high Kerr nonlinearity (n2 = 7.43 ± 0.87x10−13 cm2/W ) comparing to other silicon-based material platforms
efficient SFWM can be achieved with only millimeters of waveguide propagation
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors cite Oo et al. that the lowest reported a-Si:H linear propagation losses are about an order of magnitude higher than Si3N4, and state that this high loss leaves many photon pairs lost on chip before off-chip detection, which reduces the observable CAR.
quotes: the lowest reported a-Si:H linear propagation losses are about an order of magnitude higher than Si3N4
the high propagation loss of a-Si:H waveguide resuts in many of the photon pairs being lost on chip before off-chip detection.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to other work, with the authors' consequence stated as motivation.
assertions.reader_inference: This paper's own figures are 4 dB/cm for a-Si:H and 0.5 dB/cm for SiNx, a factor of 8.

assertions.value: The authors describe the pump as a 50 MHz mode-locked laser filtered by four cascaded DWDM filters at 1552.5 nm, coupled in the TE waveguide mode into a 2.5 mm long a-Si:H waveguide, with Stokes photons collected at 1545.3 nm and anti-Stokes photons at 1559.7 nm through 200 GHz DWDM filters.
quotes: a 50MHz mode lock laser(Calmar Mendocino)
four cascaded dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM)
at 1552.5 nm
a 2.5 mm long a-Si:H waveguide where the photon-pair is generated
at 1545.3 nm collect Stokes photons
The anti-Stokes photon at 1559.7nm is collected by two other DWDMs.
The bandwidth for the DWDM ﬁlters are aligned to be 200 GHz.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in Section 2, p.3.
assertions.reader_inference: The bandwidth of 200 GHz is stated in the sentence 'The bandwidth for the DWDM filters are aligned to be 200 GHz.'; the 50 MHz repetition rate gives the 20 ns pulse spacing used in the g2 normalization.

assertions.value: The authors report detection with 4-channel superconducting nanowire single photon detectors (ID281, ID Quantique) with a dark-count rate of 50-100 Hz and a detection efficiency of 85%, read out by a time-tagging unit from Swabian Instruments, with output DWDM sets adding 1.9 dB loss at the Stokes channel and 2.2 dB at the anti-Stokes channel, and pump rejection by two cascaded DWDM filters of labelled 60 dB extinction.
quotes: The SNSPDs have dark-count rate of 50-100 Hz and detection efficiency of 85%.
The total losses by the output DWDM sets are 1.9 dB and 2.2 dB at Stokes and anti-Stokes channels, respectively.
two cascaded DWDM
with labelled 60 dB extinction
(4 channels SNSPDs, ID281, ID Quantique)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own detection setup in Section 2, pp.3-4.
assertions.reader_inference: The 60 dB figure is the filter's label, not a measurement by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors state that SRS-generated photons in the waveguide are linearly proportional to the on-chip pump power while SFWM-generated photons scale with the square of the pump power (printed flat as Pi2n in the text layer), and that the SRS noise is extracted at the Stokes and anti-Stokes channels by fitting the single-photon count curves.
quotes: the SRS generated photons are linearly proportional to the on-chip pump power Pin while the SFWM generated photons are proportional to Pi2n.
SRS noise can be abstracted at Stokes and anti-Stokes channels by
assertions.certainty_reason: A scaling statement used to separate noise from signal; the fit itself is in Figure 3(b), which the text layer does not carry.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no fitted SRS coefficient in text.

assertions.value: The authors' comparison table compares chi(3) photon-pair sources across nine rows, listing CAR values of 399, 1632.6, 373.3, 274, 2610, 12105, 532, 2280 and 4389, for materials from a-Si:H, a-Si:H/Si3N4, c-Si disk, c-Si ring, Si3N4 ring and AlGaAsOI ring.
quotes: a-Si:H a-Si:H/Si3N4 a-Si:H/Si3N4
c-Si disk c-Si disk c-Si ring c-Si ring Si3N4 ring AlGaAsOI ring
assertions.certainty_reason: A literature comparison table assembled by the authors; the text layer flattens it by column.
assertions.reader_inference: By column order the two 'This work' rows are CAR 1632.6 at 0.9 µW with PGR 1.94 MHz, and CAR 373.3 at 5.6 µW with PGR 3.29 MHz and gH(2) 0.0126. The table lists higher CAR for a c-Si ring (12105, Ma 2017), an AlGaAsOI ring (4389, Steiner 2021) and a c-Si disk (2610, Lu 2016), so the 1632.6 record holds only within non-resonant a-Si:H waveguides, as the paper states.

assertions.value: The authors' Table 1 lists on-chip pump powers of 18 µW, 0.9 µW, 5.6 µW, 79 µW, 12µW, 7.4 µW, 59 µW, 46 µW and 3.4 µW, and photon pair generation rates of 65 kHz, 1.94 MHz, 3.29 MHz, 855 kHz, 1.2 kHz, 16 kHz, 1.1 MHz, 4.8 kHz and 230KHz.
quotes: On-chip pump power 18 µW 0.9 µW 5.6 µW 79 µW 12µW 7.4 µW 59 µW 46 µW 3.4 µW
PGR 65 kHz 1.94 MHz 3.29 MHz 855 kHz 1.2 kHz 16 kHz 1.1 MHz 4.8 kHz 230KHz
assertions.certainty_reason: A table of figures the authors collected from their own and other works; not re-measured here.
assertions.reader_inference: The 3.29 MHz pair rate at 5.6 µW in the table does not appear in the body text. The body gives the pair rate only at the CAR peak (1.94 MHz at about -30.5 dBm, which is 0.9 µW).

assertions.value: The authors state that, because the photon pairs come from a non-resonant waveguide without microring enhancement, there is more freedom of wavelength selection and the instabilities of resonance shifting due to the thermo-optic effect or nonlinear phase modulation from a strong pump are avoided.
quotes: the photon pairs can be produced efficiently through our non-resonant waveguide without the nonlinearity enhancement by microring.
This allows more freedom of wavelength selection and avoid the instabilities of resonance shifting due to the thermo-optic effect
assertions.certainty_reason: An author argument; no stability measurement is reported in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no long-term stability test. Its comparison with resonant sources in Table 1 shows those sources reach higher CAR.

assertions.value: The authors state that, with a CAR higher than 1000 and a PGR of 1.94 MHz, their device can massively produce high quality photon pairs, and they present the a-Si:H/Si3N4 platform as an excellent and stable platform for photon-pair and single-photon generation.
quotes: With the CAR higher than 1000, our work features a high PGR of 1.94 MHz.
This shows that our device can massively produce high quality photon pairs.
assertions.certainty_reason: A characterization by the authors; no figure of merit for 'massively' is defined.
assertions.reader_inference: The CAR above 1000 and the PGR of 1.94 MHz are reported at the same pump power (about -30.5 dBm); the paper does not state a CAR above 1000 at higher pair rates.

assertions.value: The authors state that the CAR over the measured detuning range showcases a wide bandwidth for photon-pair generation that can be dispersion engineered into these devices.
quotes: This showcases a wide bandwidth for photon-pair generation that can be dispersion engineered into these devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement about what can be done; no dispersion-engineered device is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that the gH(2)(τ) measurement indicates their heterogeneous chip is a versatile single and paired photon source for a variety of quantum optical information technologies, and that gH(2)(τ) is important for ensuring the purity of a photon pair source.
quotes: This gH(2)(τ ) measurement indicates our heterogeneous chip is a versatile single and paired photon sources for a variety of quantum optical information technologies.
are important for ensuring the purity of photon pair source.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author interpretation; no application is demonstrated.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper demonstrates no downstream quantum information task, no indistinguishability measurement and no entanglement measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that correlated photon-pair sources are of great interest for quantum computing, teleportation, information processing, sensing and cryptography, and that a source with a broad and switchable bandwidth is essential for quantum frequency multiplexing and quantum memory, citing prior work.
quotes: correlated photon-pair sources are of great interest due to their applications in quantum computing, quantum teleportation, quantum information processing, quantum sensing, quantum cryptography
A photon pair source with a broad and switchable bandwidth is essential for applications such as quantum frequency multiplexing and quantum memory
assertions.certainty_reason: Background statements attributed to the cited literature.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Hemsley et al., that a-Si:H can be deposited at a lower temperature than crystalline silicon and thus incorporated in massive chip manufacturing processes.
quotes: a-Si:H can be easily deposited at a lower temperature and thus incorporated in massive chip manufacturing processes
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the increased coupling efficiency and low propagation losses of the SiNx waveguide allow a higher photon detection rate at much lower on-chip pump power, which enables a high CAR and a high photon pair generation rate.
quotes: with the increased coupling efficiency and low propagation losses of the SiNx waveguide, higher photon detection rate can be observed with much lower on-chip pump power.
This enables us to achieve a high CAR and high photon pair generation rate.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion; no single-layer control device is measured in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The only comparison is with the earlier a-Si:H result from Table 1, which differs in pump, filters and detectors.

assertions.value: The authors state that the multi-material deposition and low-loss interlayer couplers offer a way to integrate components from other materials in future photonic integrated circuits, naming chi(2) nonlinearity and electro-optic modulation from lithium niobate, laser sources from III-V materials, and photodetectors from germanium.
quotes: The multi-material deposition and low-loss interlayer couplers has enabled a way to combine different materials’ features onto the single platform
for example χ2 nonlinearity and electro-optic modulation from lithium niobate, laser source from III-V materials, and photodetectors from germanium
assertions.certainty_reason: A forward-looking statement; none of these integrations is demonstrated in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The photon-pair source, pump laser, filters and SNSPDs of this work are all off-chip; only the pair generation and routing are on-chip.
